sections.heading: Title
sections.source_text: This work delivers a sharp theoretical analysis of the test error of finite-rank kernel ridge regression. Finite-rank kernels show up whenever we freeze a pre-trained network and train only its last layer, yet the standard generalization bounds become loose in exactly this regime. The authors derive matching non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the test error that stay tight for any regularization strength, including the ridgeless limit, and validate them empirically against the tangent neural tangent kernel.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.source_text: Kernel ridge regression is a workhorse for understanding generalization, and it becomes especially relevant because training the last layer of a deep network behaves like regression with a finite-rank kernel. The trouble is that classical bounds, built for general kernels, are far too loose in this finite-rank setting. They often require the ridge parameter to stay away from zero, they only supply upper bounds, and they can even become vacuous as the regularization vanishes. The paper sets out to close this gap with bounds that are actually sharp.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.source_text: Why now? Because the practical recipe of freezing a pre-trained backbone and retraining just the final layer is everywhere, from reservoir computers to few-shot learning. That recipe defines a finite-dimensional feature map, and hence a finite-rank kernel. Yet the theory available for this exact situation lags behind: many results demand the input dimension tend to infinity, others only work when the ridge decays at a prescribed rate as the sample size grows, and almost none provide a lower bound. Without a lower bound you cannot claim your upper bound is tight. This paper is motivated by the need for guarantees that are both non-asymptotic and two-sided.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.source_text: The contribution is threefold. First, unlike prior work, the new bounds actually get better as the ridge parameter goes to zero, matching the intuition that less regularization can mean less error in this setting. Second, the authors provide a sharp lower bound on the test error that provably matches their upper bound as the sample size increases, so the bounds are tight in a precise sense. Third, they validate everything empirically, showing a dramatic improvement over the closest prior bound. The technical trick that makes this possible is to work in the L-two basis of eigenfunctions rather than the reproducing-kernel basis, which decouples the kernel spectrum from the randomness of sampling.

sections.heading: Method
sections.source_text: The method starts from the ordinary kernel-ridge estimator, the minimizer of the regularized least-squares objective over the reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. The test error is defined as the expected squared deviation from the true target, and it splits cleanly into a bias term, the error with noiseless labels, and a variance term driven by label noise. The authors bound each piece with high probability. The crucial technical ingredients are more careful algebraic handling of the terms that involve the ridge, and a concentration inequality for a sub-Gaussian random covariance matrix, combined with a Neumann-series expansion of a matrix inverse. This is what lets the bounds hold for any ridge value, rather than only for a ridge that shrinks with the sample size.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.source_text: Because this is a theory paper, the experiments use controlled synthetic settings rather than large datasets. The authors evaluate on two finite-rank kernels: a truncated neural tangent kernel, which mimics the last-layer behavior of a wide network, and a separately constructed low-rank kernel. For each, they run kernel ridge regression across sample sizes from roughly ten up to two hundred, and across a sweep of ridge values, averaging over ten random trials and reporting medians with quartile error bars. These controlled settings are exactly where the true spectrum and target decomposition are known, so the derived bounds can be compared against the empirically measured test error.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.source_text: The headline result is that the new upper and lower bounds actually bracket the measured test error over the whole range of sample sizes, on both test kernels, and the two bounds squeeze together as the sample size grows, which is the empirical signature of tightness. When compared directly against the best previously known bound, due to Bach, the improvement is stark: on a log scale, the new upper bound hugs the true error while Bach's bound floats far above it, both as the sample size varies and as the inverse ridge varies. In the ridgeless limit, the analysis further shows the bias is governed purely by the irreducible finite-rank error and the variance purely by the noise level.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.source_text: The paper effectively ablates its own bound term by term. It identifies which contributions matter and which wash out. The finite-rank error term is the irreducible floor that no amount of extra data can remove, while several residue terms shrink at a log-N-over-N rate and become negligible for large samples. When those residue terms are dropped for simplicity, the simplified bounds stop bracketing the error only in the small-sample regime, exactly as the theory predicts, and they recover tightness as the sample size grows. A separate sweep over the ridge parameter isolates where the improvement comes from: the new bound keeps improving toward the ridgeless limit while the prior bound gets worse.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.source_text: A few numbers anchor the results. The bounds hold with probability at least one minus two over N, so the confidence itself sharpens as the sample grows. The upper bound decays at a log-N-over-N rate, which is an order of magnitude faster than the square-root rate you get from a generic Rademacher-complexity argument. The variance scales like the noise variance times twice the rank over the sample size, valid whenever the sample exceeds the kernel rank. And crucially, these are the first bounds to include a high-probability lower bound in this finite-rank setting, where prior work offered none.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.source_text: The one-line takeaway is that the kind of model behind last-layer fine-tuning, finite-rank kernel ridge regression, now has generalization bounds that are genuinely sharp: matching upper and lower bounds that stay tight for any amount of regularization, including none at all. That gives a far more honest certificate of test error than the loose, one-sided, asymptotic guarantees that came before, and the key idea, working in the eigenfunction basis to separate the kernel spectrum from sampling noise, is a template other finite-rank analyses can borrow.
